summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing that the IETF raise money by selling protocol field naming rights, associating commercial brands with fields. It describes a mock process for assigning rights. It is informational and not meant seriously.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke paper that says companies could pay to put their names on parts of internet rules, like naming a stadium.

questions: selling naming rights in ietf protocols
did the ietf ever sell naming rights
subtitle: Selling ad space in protocol field names (April 1st satire)

tldr.problem: The IETF's budget is tight, and meeting fees keep rising. This April 1st proposal jokingly suggests that protocol field names are valuable real estate that could generate revenue through corporate sponsorships, just like stadium naming rights.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal describes a process for selling naming rights to protocol fields: companies would bid to rename fields (e.g., the "Garmin GPS Destination Address" instead of "IPv4 Destination Address"), with taste review, auction procedures, lease terms, and mechanisms for dispute resolution.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous RFC published on April 1st, 2008. It is not a serious proposal but a tongue-in-cheek commentary on commercialization and the IETF's funding challenges. No part of this was implemented.

today: RFC 5241 is an April 1st joke RFC that remains unimplemented. The humor, while dated by a decade, captures the IETF's perennial funding challenge and the authors' wit about the value engineers place on protocol design details. No protocol field naming rights market ever emerged.

sections.title: A Modest Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 5241 is an April 1st RFC presenting a satirical proposal to monetize protocol field names. The authors note that engineers care deeply about field names ("even intensely"), and that the sports industry has made excellent use of naming rights (Staples Center, Qualcomm Stadium, Minute Maid Park). The document humorously suggests that protocol fields have commercial value and could be "sponsored."

The target audience is not protocol designers seeking revenue, but rather readers amused by the notion of seeing "the Staples Center TCP Destination Port" or "Viagra Total Length field" in a standards document.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors joke that if you put a company logo on a protocol field name, you can charge them money, just like sports stadiums do.

sections.title: How the Market Would Work
sections.content:
The proposal outlines a fictional marketplace: a taste-review process to prevent offensive pairings (though some example "bad taste" names are provided for laughs), lease terms (debated between 1-2 years for startups or 8-10 years for established firms), and pricing via auction or negotiation. The RFC Editor would publish "Real_RFCs" with branded field names prepended (e.g., "the Garmin GPS Source Address"), while archival versions kept the original names.

Disputes would be resolved using ICANN's Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy—a rule absurdist choice that perfectly fits the joke's tone.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke describes how companies would bid for naming rights, what names are "too gross," and how the IETF would manage leases and renewals.

sections.title: IANA and RFC Editor Changes
sections.content:
To implement this (hypothetically), IANA would maintain a "Protocol Field-to-Brand Name" database. The RFC Editor would convert all RFCs to XML, look up branded field names in the database, and generate ASCII "Real_RFCs" with corporate branding inserted. The document wryly notes that "[d]oing this for all existing RFCs may involve some work" and that "the software to do some of the formatting might be a bit tricky."

The document concludes with a call for future expansion to cover other protocol features like options and parameters (e.g., "the Herman Melville Jumbogram option").
sections.plainLanguage: The joke continues by describing how the whole system would actually work: IANA keeps a database, and special software rewrites RFCs with brand names plugged in.

sections.title: Why This Is a Joke
sections.content: Published on 1 April 2008, this RFC was never intended for implementation. It is Informational, not Standards Track. The authors' humor lies in the dead-serious tone—every section is meticulously structured and footnoted—applied to an absurd idea. The proposal also pokes fun at real IETF concerns: tight budgets, the need for constituency support in allocation decisions, and the tension between openness and commercialization.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole thing is a joke written to look serious. But it's a funny way of thinking about the real problem: the IETF needs money.
